content: 1. Cases of encephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy, including optic neuropathy, have been reported in patients treated with metronidazole. 2. Encephalopathy associated with cerebellar toxicity has been characterized by symptoms such as ataxia, dizziness, and dysarthria. 3. Central nervous system (CNS) lesions observed on MRI have been described in reports of encephalopathy. 4. CNS symptoms and MRI-detected lesions are generally reversible within days to weeks after discontinuation of metronidazole. 5. Peripheral neuropathy, primarily sensory in nature, has been reported and is characterized by numbness or paresthesia in the extremities. 6. Convulsive seizures have been reported in patients receiving metronidazole. 7. Cases of aseptic meningitis have been reported with metronidazole use, with symptoms occurring within hours of administration and typically resolving after discontinuation of therapy. 8. The appearance of abnormal neurologic signs and symptoms requires prompt evaluation of the benefit-risk ratio of continuing therapy. 9. Patients with hepatic impairment metabolize metronidazole more slowly, leading to its accumulation in plasma. 10. In patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), the dosage or frequency of metronidazole administration should be reduced. 11. No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment, but they should be monitored for metronidazole-associated adverse events. 12. Patients with end-stage renal disease may excrete metronidazole and its metabolites more slowly, resulting in significant accumulation of its metabolites. Monitoring for adverse events is recommended. 13. Fungal superinfections, such as candidiasis, may become more prominent during metronidazole therapy and require treatment with an antifungal agent. 14. Metronidazole should be used cautiously in patients with a history of or evidence of blood dyscrasias. 15. Mild leukopenia has been observed during metronidazole administration, but no persistent hematologic abnormalities attributable to the drug have been reported in clinical studies. 16. Total and differential leukocyte counts are recommended before and after therapy. 17. Prescribing metronidazole in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial or parasitic infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria and parasites. 18. Patients should avoid consuming alcoholic beverages or products containing propylene glycol while taking metronidazole and for at least three days afterward, as this may cause abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headaches, and flushing. 19. Patients should be counseled that metronidazole is only effective for treating bacterial and parasitic infections. 20. Patients should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment, to prevent reduced effectiveness and the development of drug-resistant bacteria. 21. Tumors affecting the liver, lung, mammary, and lymphatic tissues have been observed in animal studies involving rats and mice treated with metronidazole, but not in hamsters. 22. Pulmonary tumors have been reported in all six studies conducted in mice, including one study with intermittent dosing. 23. Malignant liver tumors were increased in male mice treated with doses comparable to the maximum recommended human dose. 24. Malignant lymphomas and pulmonary neoplasms were increased with lifetime feeding of metronidazole in mice. 25. Mammary and hepatic tumors were increased in female rats administered oral metronidazole compared to controls. 26. Two lifetime tumorigenicity studies in hamsters were negative. 27. Metronidazole has shown mutagenic activity in in vitro assay systems, such as the Ames test, but in vivo studies in mammals have not demonstrated genetic damage. 28. Metronidazole did not adversely affect fertility or testicular function in male rats treated for 28 days at doses comparable to the maximum recommended human dose. 29. However, rats treated for six weeks or longer showed infertility, severe degeneration of seminiferous epithelium, and marked decreases in sperm counts. Fertility was restored in most rats after an eight-week drug-free recovery period. 30. Metronidazole is classified as Pregnancy Category B. 31. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of metronidazole in pregnant women. 32. Published data from studies involving over 5,000 pregnant women, including first-trimester exposures, have not consistently shown an increased risk of congenital abnormalities or adverse fetal outcomes. 33. One study suggested an increased risk of cleft lip, with or without cleft palate, but these findings were not confirmed. 34. Randomized clinical trials assessing antibiotic treatment, including metronidazole, for bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy did not show an increased risk of congenital abnormalities. 35. Metronidazole crosses the placental barrier, and its effects on human fetal organogenesis are unknown. 36. Reproduction studies in animals have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus at doses comparable to the maximum recommended human dose. 37. Metronidazole is present in human milk at concentrations similar to maternal serum levels, and infant serum levels can approach therapeutic levels. 38. Due to the potential for tumorigenicity observed in animal studies, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 39. Alternatively, nursing mothers may pump and discard milk during therapy and for 24 hours after therapy ends, feeding the infant stored milk or formula. 40. In geriatric patients, monitoring for metronidazole-associated adverse events is recommended. 41. Decreased liver function in elderly patients may result in increased concentrations of metronidazole, necessitating dosage adjustments. 42. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established, except for the treatment of amebiasis.
